ROUNDUP

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
.....banned elsewhere in the world, a cancer causing chemical is freely available in South Africa for use in homes and on farms

Unique Selling Point:
The story is about an unregulated, dangerous chemical. And that is just the tip of the ice-berg.

Summary:
Bayer's 'Roundup' weedkiller contains glyphosate as its main active ingredient. The herbicide has been at the centre of a class action lawsuit in the US, in which more than 100 000 people have claimed that the product caused them to develop cancer. But roundup is used widely in homes and in agriculture in South Africa. Even Government is using it. Despite the dangers, it is still not banned here.


Further information:
Bayer is spending $11 billion (R163 billion) on settling 96 000 claims and has set aside an additional $4.5 billion (R25 billion) for future claims.

Since the US ruling a number US states and countries worldwide have banned the use of Roundup.

Others that have previously banned the substance are eg Belgium, Bermuda Colombia The Netherlands Sri Lanka El Salvador Middle Eastern countries including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman and the United Arab Emirates France.

In about a year, US consumers will be able to buy glyphosate-free Roundup herbicide for their homes and gardens.

But the contentious active ingredient will continue to be included in the product used in South Africa. It is for sale in supermarkets and garden supply stores, and used widely in agriculture.

Traces of glyphosate has been found in a large number of animal and plant products on supermarket shelves in South Africa.

The South African government has previously said in 2015 glyphosate-based products that are registered in the country go through a rigorous process and pose minimal risk to users, if used according to instructions on the label. The Dept of Environmental Affairs uses it and also sprays it on water sources.

However, there is a growing corpus of literature and experts that say it should be banned completely. Symptoms of glyphosate poisoning are;

Abdominal cramps.
Anxiety.
Breathing difficulty.
Coma.
Blue lips or fingernails (rare)
Diarrhea.
Dizziness.
Drowsiness.

It is also linked to Hodgkin lymphoma

Glyphosate, which is used extensively in South Africa, causes deformation to the reproductive shape of plants, which could have wide-ranging effects on pollinator species, foraging animals and people, experts say.


INTERVIEWEES

Angela Andrews -- Environmental lawyer who says the big problem in South Africa is our current and very outdated legislation.

Cansa: Professor Michael Herbst says that glyphosate is not toxic by itself. "But as soon as you include glyphosate in a mixture [such as Roundup] it becomes highly toxic and it causes cancer – there is no doubt about it."

Prof David Eastmond, University of California, Riverside, Expert of glyphosate and toxicology.

Case study #1: Anonymous farmer in Limpopo, sick, tested positive for poisons, severely affected by it.

Case study #2: Margaret Piedt, a farmworker who is affected by agrichemicals and who lost her husband. Anecdotal testimony.

Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD).

Bayer South Africa, manufacturer of Roundup


Extra Budget Items:
Shoot in Western Cape and limpopo.

Case Study:
Margaret Piedt

Expert:
Prof. David Eastmond
Prof. Michael Herbst
Ms. Angela Andrews

Locations:
Cape Town

Legal: Yes
Reason for legal: Allegations are made against the government, there is an issues about regulations and legislation.

Script:


V/O:
Part of South Africa’s beauty lies in what is grown in its rich soil. From wheat fields in the Swartland to the vineyards of the Western Cape to the lush maize crops waving in the wind in the Free State.

However, an essential part of growing crops on this scale is the abundant use of poisons to control pests and unwanted weeds and grasses. They are known as agrichemicals and many of them are highly toxic and even lethal to humans.

So, one would assume that there are very strict regulations around unleashing these toxins, and that there is strong enforcement to ensure that the public’s right to a safe and healthy environment is not jeopardised.

It is indeed like that in many other countries, but disturbingly, not in South Africa. Angela Andrews is an environmental lawyer from Cape Town and she claims our legislation is the major problem.

Claire:
What is our legislation when it comes to agrichemicals?

Angela:
Well, the current legislation dates back to 1947 and it says it was enacted by the King’s Most Excellent Majesty. And not withstanding the Constitution, it has not been changed.

V/O:
So, the legislation to control some of the most toxic substances unleashed in the South African air, is seventy four years old.

Angela:
What’s wrong with it? It doesn’t mention health, it doesn’t mention the protection of the environment. It merely enables the registration and sale of extremely hazardous chemicals.

V/O:
Because it pre-dates the Constitution, it is not geared to protect human rights like health and the right to a safe environment. Consequently, people all over South Africa could be harm by the current use of pesticides.

Margaret:
That spray is very dangerous. When the people spray with the tractors, and when you pass, you can still smell that the poison. And when you take it in, you feel a little bit dizzy. You feel a little bit sick. and you can feel your body's not OK and the joints also is not working very well. Sometimes you can feel it for two or three days.

VO:
Margaret Piedt, now a widow, lives near Rawsonville. She is convinced that her husband’s early death was caused by prolonged and direct exposure to pesticides.

Margret:
When he used to come by the house, he take the clothes off before he enter the house because he said the clothes is very dangerous because the clothes are full of poison.

V/O:
The passed away two years ago.

And our aged legislation is also unable to adequately deal with the most notorious and controversial agrichemical in the world - glyphosate. It is the active ingredient in a large number of weed killers.

LINK:
The most well-known of these is Roundup which is used widely in the agricultural sector, but you can also buy it for home use in supermarkets.

V/O:
Roundup is the world’s most popular herbicide, and generates billions of dollars for its manufacturer, Bayer.

In South Africa Roundup is used by farmers, but it is also used widely by homeowners, municipalities, schools and parks.

But the glyphosate in this popular weedkiller has been found by courts in the United States to non-Hogkin Lymploma, a form of cancer.

Professor David Eastmond is a Molecular, Cell & Systems Biologist at the University of California, Riverside.

Eastmond:
In 2015 one agency of the WHO convened to evaluate whether glyphosate can cause cancer. Ad they concluded that it was a probable human carcinogen.
V/O:
The agency that made the finding is the International Agency for Research on Cancer or IARC whose research is regarded as the benchmark for determining what agents might be cancer causing.

This sparked a slew of court cases in the United States and several courts found that Roundup was the cause of cancer in in the applicants.

Eventually, in May 2021 Bayer agreed to settle ninety-six thousand cancer claims for more than two hundred billion rand.

In addition, it has been found that glyphosate also poses a real threat to the environment.
LINK:
In November 2020 the United States Environmental Protection Agency stated that Roundup is likely to injure or kill 93% of the plants and animals protected under the endangered species Act.
V/O:
Roundup has over the last few years become so controversial that is has been banned in about 20 countries around the world and even in jurisdictions where authorities have not banned it, communities have begun to step in.
Eastmond:
There are a number of communities in the Unites States that are banning glyphosate or making it much more difficult to use. The University of California has basically put into place severe restrictions on glyphosate.
V/O:
The findings that glyphosate is cancer causing have been disputed by many role players in the industry who do not subscribe to the World Health Organization findings. In South Africa the Department of Agriculture has stated in 2015 that glyphosate is safe.

However, in August 2021 the Cancer Association of South Africa issued a 24-page position statement on glyphosate. Professor Michael Herbst of Cansa authored the study.

Herbst:
Glyphoste in itself does not seem to be the real problem. But the moment it comes in formulation, with all the other chemicals added to it, that seems to make the combination of carcinogenicity.

V/O:
And Roundup is singled out in the report.

Herbst:
I am totally convinced that glyphosate in formulation in the form of Roundup is definitely a cause of cancer in humans. The evidence is there. It has been proven.

V/O:
We approached Bayer in South Africa for comments and they replied:

When it comes to safety assessments, glyphosate is among the most extensively tested herbicides on the market. Evaluations spanning more than 40 years, and the overwhelming conclusion of experts and regulators worldwide, support the safety of glyphosate and that glyphosate does not cause cancer. Bayer’s position is that glyphosate-based products are safe when used as directed and that glyphosate does not pose a carcinogenic risk.

V/O:
We asked the Department of Agriculture what their current position on glyphosate is, but after numerous e-mails, telephone calls and Whatapp messages, over a period of 2 weeks, they failed to answer any of our questions.

Back in 2015 statement they indicated that if label instructions are followed, glyphosate poses “a minimal risk to users and the general public”.

But even referring to label instructions can be problematic. Because our legislation is so old, there are no statutory guidelines as to what minimum information should be on the label of a poisonous agrichemical. Consequently, labels are quite vague and non-specific.

Angela:
Now if a label says “Do not allow drift into water bodies, is a canal a waterbody? What is a waterbody? You can imagine interpretation of this thing will be very difficult.

V/O:
And it is the lack of clarity on instruction labels that nearly cost him his life, says Francois, a farmer from Limpopo with two young children. He asked to remain anonymous for fear of retaliation from agrichemical suppliers. A year ago he started to experience increasing spells of dizziness, respiratory problems, extreme fatigue and severe headaches.
Francois:
Dit het oor ‘n tydperk van maande al hoe erger geword. Dit het gevoel of ek besig is om dood te gaan. Ek het nie geweet wat aangaan nie. Ek het net aan my seuns gedink.
V/O:
Eventually tests that could only be done overseas, revealed extremely high levels of toxic substances in his blood. He was slowly being poisoned by a cocktail of dozens of chemicals, all of them originating in the pesticides and herbicides he was using on a daily basis. These included glyphosate.
Francois:
Ek werk al vir 17 jaar amper elke dag met gif op die plaas. Die aanwysings op die houers is glad nie duidelik nie en gee eintlik baie min riglyne. Ons is nou meer versigting, maar ons kan nie sonder gif boer nie, veral nie sonder Roundup nie.
V/O:
The Courts in the US have found that people developed cancer because of long-term exposure to glyphosate.

But not only farmers and farmworkers have long term exposure to glyphosate, millions of South Africans are also subjected to long term glyphosate contamination -- through the food we consume.

Studies have shown that 80% of bread sold in South Africa contains traces of glyphosate, and fifty three of eighty one supermarket products containing maize or soy have low levels of glyphosate.

This means that you could be giving your baby a dose of glyphosate with her soy baby formula or that the sandwiches in your child’s lunch box could contain this potentially cancer causing chemical.
V/O:
Unfortunately, our current severely outdated legislation is not much help to properly protect the people of South Africa against hazardous chemicals, and to address and deal with the issues around Roundup we are facing today.

Our legislation merely makes provision for the establishment of a registrar’s office and gives no guidelines for its functioning.
LINK:
So the big problem is that although there is a registrar, there are no clear criteria provided in the legislation to enable the registrar to properly evaluate applications and register herbicides and pesticides.
V/O:
And it gives no guidelines of how to evaluate chemicals that are in use, but found to be problematic elswhere, like Roundup.
Angela:
If that guidance is not there, the Constitutional court has said the legislation is unconstitutional.
V/O:
And this means that unless our outdated and possibly unconstitutional legislation is overhauled, the problematic status quo around the use of agrichemicals in South Africa will persist.

Others that have previously banned the substance are eg Belgium, Bermuda Colombia The Netherlands Sri Lanka El Salvador Middle Eastern countries including Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain, Oman and the United Arab Emirates France. In about a year, US consumers will be able to buy glyphosate-free Roundup herbicide for their homes and gardens. But the contentious active ingredient will continue to be included in the product used in South Africa. It is for sale in supermarkets and garden supply stores, and used widely in agriculture. Traces of glyphosate has been found in a large number of animal and plant products on supermarket shelves in South Africa. The South African government has previously said in 2015 glyphosate-based products that are registered in the country go through a rigorous process and pose minimal risk to users, if used according to instructions on the label. The Dept of Environmental Affairs uses it and also sprays it on water sources. However, there is a growing corpus of literature and experts that say it should be banned completely. Symptoms of glyphosate poisoning are; Abdominal cramps. Anxiety. Breathing difficulty. Coma. Blue lips or fingernails (rare) Diarrhea. Dizziness. Drowsiness. It is also linked to Hodgkin lymphoma Glyphosate, which is used extensively in South Africa, causes deformation to the reproductive shape of plants, which could have wide-ranging effects on pollinator species, foraging animals and people, experts say. INTERVIEWEES Angela Andrews -- Environmental lawyer who says the big problem in South Africa is our current and very outdated legislation. Cansa: Professor Michael Herbst says that glyphosate is not toxic by itself. "But as soon as you include glyphosate in a mixture [such as Roundup] it becomes highly toxic and it causes cancer – there is no doubt about it." Prof David Eastmond, University of California, Riverside, Expert of glyphosate and toxicology. Case study #1: Anonymous farmer in Limpopo, sick, tested positive for poisons, severely affected by it. Case study #2: Margaret Piedt, a farmworker who is affected by agrichemicals and who lost her husband. Anecdotal testimony. Department of Agriculture, Land Reform and Rural Development (DALRRD). Bayer South Africa, manufacturer of Roundup
